en: The Apadāna of the Elder Ekachattiya Bhaddāli-vagga 2.1 [Verse 1] When I was a king named Chatta, I gave a single white parasol to the Buddha Vipassī, who was endowed with the thirty-two marks. [Verse 2] For that deed, having passed through many births, I have never been born in a low family; I have always been born in a high family, possessing great wealth and power. [Verse 3] Having lived for a hundred thousand aeons, I have never experienced suffering; having performed that meritorious deed, I have attained this state of peace. [Verse 4] In the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, I was a monk named Chatta; having practiced the holy life under the Teacher, I was reborn in the Brahma-world. [Verse 5] From there, passing away from that state, I was reborn in Sāvatthī; there I saw the Teacher, the Blessed One, the supreme Buddha. [Verse 6] Having seen the Teacher, the Blessed One, the supreme Buddha, I offered a single white parasol to the Conqueror. [Verse 7] Because of that root of merit, I have never been born in a low family; I have always been born in a high family, possessing great wealth and power. [Verse 8] Having lived for a hundred thousand aeons, I have never experienced suffering; having performed that meritorious deed, I have attained this state of peace. [Verse 9] Now, having heard the Dhamma of the Teacher, the supreme Buddha, I have abandoned all defilements and attained Parinibbāna. [Verse 10] This is my final birth; there will be no further existence for me. Having reached the end of the round of rebirths, I shall attain Parinibbāna. [Verse 11] This is the true nature of the Dhamma of the Buddhas: for one who has done good deeds, there is no sorrow in the next world. [Verse 12] This is the fruit of giving a single white parasol; having given it to the Conqueror, I have attained this state of peace. [Verse 13] I am the Elder Ekachattiya; I have fulfilled my purpose. Having reached the end of the round of rebirths, I shall attain Parinibbāna. "On the bank of the Candabhāgā River,
my hermitage is well-prepared;
it is strewn with very pure sand."
A leaf-hut was well-constructed.
There was a river with shallow banks,
beautiful and with excellent landing places.
Abounding with fish and tortoises,
frequented by crocodiles,
and filled with hyenas, leopards, and peacocks.
The karavīka and the sāḷika birds always warble,
beautifying my hermitage.
Cuckoos with sweet voices and swans with melodious notes warble there.
Adorning my hermitage:
lions, tigers, and boars,
bears, hyenas, and jackals.
In the mountain fastnesses they cry out,
beautifying my hermitage;
the enīmiga deer and the sarabha, too.
Many bheraṇḍas and boars roar in the mountain fastness,
beautifying my hermitage.
Uddālakas and campakas,
pāṭalis and sinduvārakas;
atimuttas and asokas, too.
They beautify my hermitage:
the aṅkola, the yūthikā,
the sattalī, and the bimbijālikā.
And the kaṇikāra trees are in bloom,
beautifying my hermitage;
so too the nāga, sāla, and saḷala trees.
Here, lotuses are in full bloom;
wafting a divine fragrance,
they beautify my hermitage.
The *ajjuna* and *asana* trees here,
and the *mahānāma*;
the *sāla* and the *kaṅgupuppha*.
They beautify my hermitage:
mangoes, rose-apples, and tilakas,
neem trees, and the beautiful sal trees.
Exuding a divine fragrance,
they beautify my hermitage—
the *asoka* trees and the *kapiṭṭha* trees.
Here, the mountain garlands are in bloom;
wafting a divine fragrance,
they beautify my hermitage.
The kadamba, the plantain,
and the isimugga trees that have been planted surely bear fruit.
They beautify my hermitage:
harītaka, āmalaka,
mango, jambu, and vibhītaka.
In my hermitage there are kolā, bhallātaka, and bilva trees, as well as fruit-bearing trees;
not far away is a lotus pond.
Well-established and delightful,
they are covered with mandārava flowers and with lotuses and water-lilies.
The lotuses conceive fruit,
others blossom with filaments,
and there are those with petals and pericarps.
In my hermitage, the fish are blooming: the pāṭhīna, the pāvusa,
the balaja, the muñja, and the rohita.
Wandering in the Acchoda Lake,
they beautify my hermitage;
there are also those with the fragrance of mangoes.
And the *ketaka* trees,
blowing with their divine fragrance,
beautify my hermitage.
Honey flows from the lotus roots,
milk and ghee from the lilies;
wafting forth a divine fragrance, they spread abroad.
They beautify my hermitage. There,
the sandy shores are beautiful,
strewn with [treasures] and frequented by water-dwellers.
The flowers, in full bloom, lie scattered about,
beautifying my hermitage.
Burdened by the weight of matted locks, they remain.
Clad in upper garments of antelope skin,
all of them wearing bark and rags,
they beautify my hermitage.
Looking ahead only as far as a yoke’s length,
prudent and living in peace,
they are indifferent toward the enjoyments of sensual desire.
They dwell in my hermitage,
with the hair of their armpits and navels grown long,
their teeth stained with grime, and their heads covered in dust.
All of them, wearing dust and dirt,
dwell in my hermitage;
they have attained perfection in the higher knowledges.
And they are wanderers of the sky;
rising into the heavens,
they beautify my hermitage.
Surrounded by those disciples,
I was then dwelling in the forest;
I did not distinguish between night and day.
At that time, the Blessed One, the great sage who perceives the meaning, was constantly absorbed in jhāna.
Dispelling that darkness,
the Leader of the World arose;
then a certain disciple—
He came into my presence,
desiring to study the sixfold science of marks known as *Lakkhaṇa*.
The Buddha has arisen in the world,
the great sage Atthadassi,
proclaiming the Four Noble Truths.
He teaches the deathless state.
Elated, joyful, and delighted,
his heart has found its refuge within the Dhamma.
Having gone forth from the household life,
I spoke these words:
"A Buddha has arisen in the world."
Possessing the thirty-two marks of excellence;
come, let us all go into the presence of the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
They accepted the instruction,
having reached perfection in the True Dhamma,
and responded, "Excellent!"
Seekers of the supreme goal,
burdened by masses of matted hair and clad in deerskins as upper garments.
Seeking the supreme goal,
they then departed from the forest.
At that time, the Blessed One—
Atthadassi, of great renown,
proclaiming the Four Noble Truths,
teaches the deathless state.
Having taken a white parasol,
I held it over the Best of Buddhas;
having held it for a single day, I—
I paid homage to the Best of Buddhas.
Then the Blessed One Atthadassī,
the Eldest in the World, the Bull among Men;
Having sat down in the community of bhikkhus,
he spoke these verses:
“He who held the sunshade for me— ”
With serene and wholesome hands,
I shall extol him;
listen as I speak.
As he was being born,
whether in the state of a god or a human,
he shall always bear the parasol.
This is the fruit of the gift of a parasol:
for seventy-seven eons,
he shall delight in the world of the gods.
A thousand times he will become a wheel-turning monarch,
and seventy-seven times as well.
He will exercise sovereignty over the gods;
his local sovereignty will be vast and beyond counting.
In eighteen hundred kappas,
Gotama, the bull of the Sakyas,
shall dispel that darkness.
One with vision will arise.
He is the heir to the Dhamma,
the legitimate son, fashioned by the Dhamma.
"Having fully understood all taints,
he will dwell free from taints"—
this was the deed that I performed.
Holding the parasol for the Buddha;
in this interval, I do not know of any white parasol that was not held [for him].
"This is my final one;
my last existence is now unfolding;
even while holding the royal parasol,"
It proceeds at all times. "Oh,
how well-performed was the deed by me for Atthadassi, the Tathāgata!"
All taints are utterly destroyed;
there is now no further becoming.
The defilements have been burnt away by me.
I dwell free from taints.
Welcome indeed has come to me!
... [as before] ... the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) have been attained.
the Buddha’s teaching has been accomplished.
Thus indeed did the Venerable Ekachattiya Thera speak these verses.
The legend of the Elder Ekachattiya is the second.
